🇷🇺🇨🇳🇺🇸 The new space race: nuclear reactors on the Moon

The United States, China and Russia are competing for control of the Moon, and the key to that contest is nuclear power, The New York Times reports.

Whoever builds the first lunar base gains access to resources such as frozen water and a launchpad for missions deeper into the solar system. Both Washington and Beijing see a reactor as "the centerpiece of this ambition."

In late August, NASA asked contractors to prepare a reactor able to survive the flight and run without maintenance near the Moon's south pole. The agency wants it ready to launch by December 2030.

China and Russia are working together, and on the nuclear side Russia has the lead role. According to the NYT, Russia is the world leader in civilian nuclear power, has put more than 30 reactors into orbit, and holds the largest stocks of nuclear fuel suitable for space missions, which the Americans are badly short of.

Moscow has ordered its agencies to build a lunar reactor called "Selena" by 2036 to power the stations China is building. It is designed to run autonomously for a decade and shares features with an earlier reactor developed for the Arctic.

Leading scientists warn that governments are moving too fast, especially given the risk of a launch accident in the atmosphere. The US and Russia say their reactors will stay switched off until they reach the Moon, and engineers argue that "cold" uranium fuel poses little radioactive threat even if it falls back to Earth.

As for the Moon itself, both NASA and the Russian agencies say they will simply leave the radioactive material there.

Pura Ulun Danu Beratan, Indonesia

A journey to Bali—often called the Island of the Gods—isn’t truly complete without experiencing its sacred temples, and Pura Ulun Danu Beratan stands as one of the most unforgettable.

Perched gracefully on the shores of Lake Beratan, the temple appears to float amid misty mountain peaks at 3,900 feet above sea level. The panoramic views are nothing short of breathtaking.

Surrounding the area are thriving organic farms and colorful nurseries bursting with marigolds, hydrangeas, and other blooms, adding life and vibrancy to the cool highland air.

Constructed in 1633, this revered site honors Dewi Danu, the goddess of water, and holds a central place among Bali’s nine directional temples. 

Since Lake Beratan feeds irrigation systems for nearby agriculture, the temple remains spiritually and practically vital to local communities.
